items.caption: z and z̄ mirrored in the real axis, |z| = 3.6
items.text: The point z and its conjugate z̄ sit at the same distance from the origin, one above the real axis and one below: conjugation keeps the real part and flips the sign of the imaginary part, so it is a reflection in the real axis. items.caption: Four roots for a degree-4 equation
items.text: The example from the text: z⁴ = −1 has no solution on the real line, yet in the plane it has exactly four, as the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra promises for degree 4. All four have modulus 1, so they sit on the unit circle, and their arguments 45°, 135°, 225°, 315° are 90° apart. Because the coefficients are real, the roots come in conjugate pairs — each is the mirror image of another across the real axis.

items.text: z = 3i sits on the imaginary axis, three units above the origin, so |z| = √(0² + 3²) = 3. Its conjugate −3i sits three units below and has the same modulus: on the imaginary axis, as on the real axis, the modulus is the distance from 0 and ignores the sign. items.page: Additive Inverse: Negation of Complex Numbers
items.caption: z and −z through the origin
items.text: Negating both coordinates of z = 3 + 2i gives −z = −3 − 2i, the point directly opposite through 0. The two sit at the ends of one diameter of the circle of radius |z| = √13, so |−z| = |z|, and the origin is their midpoint. The curved arrow is the half turn about 0 that carries z to −z: the argument grows by exactly 180°.

items.page: Algebraic Form: Standard Form a + bi
items.caption: z and z̄ mirrored in the real axis, |z| = 3.6
items.text: The point z and its conjugate z̄ sit at the same distance from the origin, one above the real axis and one below: conjugation keeps the real part and flips the sign of the imaginary part, so it is a reflection in the real axis. items.caption: z · z̄ lands on the positive real axis

items.caption: The three cube roots of 8
items.text: Write 8 = 8 cis 0°. Every cube root has modulus 8^(1/3) = 2, so all three sit on the circle of radius 2. Their arguments are (0° + 360°k)/3 for k = 0, 1, 2: 0°, 120° and 240°. The real root 2 is the one real-number experience finds; the other two, −1 ± √3 i, are a conjugate pair, and each cubes to 8 because tripling 120° or 240° lands on a multiple of 360°.

items.caption: Three linear factors, three roots
items.text: Each linear factor of z³ − 1 is one root in the plane: 1 on the real axis, and ω, ω² at 120° and 240° on the unit circle. Over the reals only the factor z − 1 splits off; the other two roots are a conjugate pair, and multiplying their factors gives (z − ω)(z − ω²) = z² + z + 1, which has real coefficients but no real root.

items.caption: The n + 2 solutions for n = 2
items.text: Matching moduli in z² = z̄ gives r² = r, so r = 0 or r = 1. The case r = 0 is the single point z = 0, drawn filled. The case r = 1 puts the rest on the unit circle, where matching arguments gives 3θ = 360°k: three solutions at 0°, 120° and 240°. That makes 1 + 3 = 4 = n + 2, two more than the n roots of zⁿ = w.

items.secTitle: The Exponential Form of a Complex Number
items.caption: z = 2e^(iπ/3)
items.text: The exponential form reads as directions for reaching z: turn to the angle θ = π/3, then go out a distance r = 2. The factor e^(iθ) supplies the direction on the unit circle and r stretches it, so the point lands on the circle of radius 2, with coordinates r cos θ = 1 and r sin θ = √3 — the algebraic form 1 + √3 i. items.caption: z and z̄ mirrored in the real axis, |z| = 3.6
items.text: The point z and its conjugate z̄ sit at the same distance from the origin, one above the real axis and one below: conjugation keeps the real part and flips the sign of the imaginary part, so it is a reflection in the real axis. The modulus, the length of either arrow, is the same 3.6 for both. Drag z anywhere and watch its mirror image follow on the

items.caption: Mirror pair — (2+2i) & (−2+2i), frozen
items.text: Sum 4i straight up, difference 4 straight right: real parts cancel in the sum, imaginary parts cancel in the difference. Equal moduli make the parallelogram a rhombus with perpendicular diagonals.

items.caption: (4+2i)/(1−i), frozen
items.text: Subtracting the −45° denominator angle swings the quotient up to 71.6°: the teal 1 + 3i sits higher than either input. Dividing by a downward-pointing number rotates the result upward.
